title: Trail running injury risk factors: a living systematic review
authors: Viljoen C, Janse van Rensburg DCC, van Mechelen W, Verhagen E, Silva B, Scheer V, et al.
population: Trail runners in 19 eligible studies (10 on injury risk factors, 2,785 participants); searches to 18 March 2021; living review with updates every 6 months
findings: 19 studies included; 10 investigated injury risk factors among 2,785 participants.
Significant intrinsic factors associated with injury: more running experience, level A runner, higher PAD-22 score.
Significant extrinsic factors associated with injury: neglecting warm-up, no specialised running plan, training on asphalt, double training sessions per day, physical labour occupations.
Injury incidence 0.7-61.2 per 1000 hours of running; prevalence 1.3%-90%; the lower limb, specifically blisters of the foot or toe, was the most reported region.
Authors conclude that limited studies investigated injury risk factors in trail running.
More than 3 hours of training per day was associated with sunburn, not injury.
limitations: Few, heterogeneous studies. The abstract lists no training-load progression or elevation factor, and the abstract does not say whether those were studied. Later updates of this living review may exist and were not checked. Abstract-level verification only.
implications: The abstract lists no tested ascent, descent or load-progression factor, so there is no trail-specific evidence here for a spike or ramp threshold; extending road-based limits to trail and ultra training is a convention.
'No specialised running plan' was associated with more injury in trail runners, a weak argument for giving structured plans, not for a particular progression.
More running experience was associated with injury here, in line with not loosening limits automatically for experienced runners.
Absence of evidence, not evidence of safety: no study links a given longest-run length or back-to-back to injury, so injury cannot justify either a 6 h cap or its removal.
'No specialised running plan' and 'double sessions per day' as risk factors mildly favour a structured plan and caution on same-day doubles.
